name: Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models
title: Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models
answer: Keeping financial data out of public models covers the controls and practices that stop sensitive financial information from being entered into, retained by, or used to train AI services that are open to the public. The data in scope includes client identities, account numbers, transaction records, trading positions, payroll, invoices, ledgers, forecasts, and material non-public information, along with any text that could reveal them. The models in scope include hosted chat assistants, public APIs, code assistants, and any third-party tool that may log prompts or use them for improvement. The work also touches data classification, vendor contracts, employee use policies, and the boundary between private model deployments and public endpoints. It sits inside the broader governance, risk, and financial data security field, where compliance and legal activity around AI is growing.

The data in scope includes client identities, account numbers, transaction records, trading positions, payroll, invoices, ledgers, forecasts, and material non-public information, along with any text that could reveal them. The models in scope include hosted chat assistants, public APIs, code assistants, and any third-party tool that may log prompts or use them for improvement. The work also touches data classification, vendor contracts, employee use policies, and the boundary between private model deployments and public endpoints. It sits inside the broader governance, risk, and financial data security field, where compliance and legal activity around AI is growing.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The infrastructure for keeping financial data out of public models runs on data classification and tagging systems, data loss prevention tools, identity and access management, and secure network gateways that inspect traffic to AI endpoints. Teams often deploy private model instances in a virtual private cloud or on-premises GPU clusters, using services such as Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, or Google Vertex AI with data isolation settings, or open-weight models like Llama and Mistral run locally. Tokenization vaults, key management services, and masking proxies replace sensitive fields with surrogate values before any prompt leaves the controlled environment. Logging, monitoring, and egress controls record what was sent and block attempts to paste restricted data into public tools. Retrieval augmented generation can be configured with permission-aware indexes so that a model only sees documents the user is already allowed to access.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done through a repeatable cycle of inventory, classification, control, and monitoring. Teams map where financial data lives and which AI tools employees use, then classify each data set and each use case by sensitivity and regulatory exposure. Controls include redaction, masking, tokenization, pseudonymization, and synthetic data generation, applied before data reaches any model, along with prompt filtering and output scanning to catch accidental disclosures. Vendor assessments, data processing agreements, and model cards document what a provider does with inputs and whether those inputs train future models. Audit trails, red teaming, and incident response procedures test the controls and record what happened when something slips through.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights, risk, and provenance in this area turn on who owns the data, what contracts and regulations allow, and whether a model can forget what it has seen. Financial firms have confidentiality duties to clients, purpose limitation and erasure rights under privacy laws, and recordkeeping rules that may conflict with deleting data from a model. Risks include prompt injection, model inversion, membership inference, shadow AI use, and vendor terms that permit training on customer inputs. Provenance requires data lineage, consent records, retention schedules, and logs of prompts and outputs, because a public model that has already trained on a piece of data cannot easily unlearn it. The site tracks 219 compliance and regulation pages and 148 active AI lawsuits, which gives a sense of the surrounding activity.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more private and controlled model deployments, stronger contractual protections, and clearer technical standards for data handling. Regulators in several jurisdictions are moving on AI-specific rules, and financial supervisors are asking for evidence of controls rather than promises. Confidential computing, federated learning, differential privacy, and data clean rooms are maturing as ways to use data without exposing it. Smaller, locally hosted models and retrieval systems that respect existing permissions are reducing the need to send sensitive data to public endpoints. The site's 686 glossary terms and 732 AI tools reflect how quickly the vocabulary and the vendor market are expanding, which keeps governance teams busy mapping new options to old obligations.
